summary: Documents the Not-So-Stubby Area option for OSPF. An NSSA is like an OSPF stub area but can still import some external routes in a limited way. It builds on the earlier definition in RFC 1587, with changes that expand capability while staying backward-compatible, so implementations of both interoperate.

eli5.summary: Some neighborhoods in a road network are normally closed to outside roads. This lets a few special outside roads connect in anyway, in a small controlled way.

questions: how do nssa areas import external routes
subtitle: An OSPF area that stays small like a stub area but can still bring in some outside routes.

tldr.problem: OSPF stub areas keep routing tables small, but a stub area cannot import routes from outside OSPF, so a site that learns external routes (for example from RIP) cannot be a stub.
tldr.mechanism: An NSSA adds an N option bit and a new Type-7 LSA that carries external routes inside the area only. NSSA border routers translate selected Type-7 LSAs into Type-5 LSAs and flood them to the rest of the OSPF domain.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3101 obsoletes RFC 1587. Its changes expand capability but are backward-compatible, so implementations of both interoperate.

today: RFC 3101 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1587. The metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Not-So-Stubby Areas Exist
sections.content:
The RFC gives two motivating cases. In the first, a wide-area transit network has "leaf" sites whose networks are learned by RIP on a site router (the RFC calls it BR18). Such a cloud looks like an OSPF stub area, which would keep external routes off the low-speed link and abstract the transit network behind a default route. But OSPF's original rules make it illegal for a stub area to import routes external to OSPF, so the transit network could only run OSPF out to its own router and had to run RIP on the last link.

In the second, a corporate network has non-zero areas that want to be stub areas to keep their link state databases small. They also want to originate aggregated external advertisements for subnets such as 192.168.192/20 and 192.168.208/22, with each area preferring a different border router. A plain stub area has no way to redistribute such routes or to aggregate external routes.
sections.eli5: A quiet cul-de-sac wants to stay small and simple, but one house on it has a private driveway to a different town. The old rules said no outside driveways on a cul-de-sac, so this adds a careful exception.

sections.title: The NSSA Design
sections.content:
OSPF area configurations come in two classes: areas that flood Type-5 LSAs (called Type-5 capable areas, which can carry transit traffic and always include the backbone) and stub areas that do not. A not-so-stubby area (NSSA) is defined much like a stub area, with a new option bit (the N bit) and a new LSA type (Type-7).

Type-7 LSAs carry external routes within an NSSA. They have virtually the same syntax as Type-5 LSAs and are flooded only inside one NSSA. Type-5 LSAs are not flooded into an NSSA and do not originate there. To let external information cross the border, NSSA border routers translate selected Type-7 LSAs into Type-5 LSAs, which are flooded to all Type-5 capable areas. Address ranges can be configured so that several Type-7 LSAs are aggregated into one Type-5 LSA.

An NSSA border router should also originate a default LSA for 0.0.0.0/0 into the NSSA, since an NSSA does not receive full routing information. Like stub areas, NSSAs may attach to Area 0 at more than one border router but may not be used as a transit area.
sections.eli5: Inside the cul-de-sac, outside roads get a special color on the map. A gatekeeper at the entrance repaints the chosen ones in the normal color before sharing them with the rest of the town.

sections.title: The N-bit, P-bit and Type-7 LSAs
sections.content:
The N-bit makes sure all routers in an NSSA agree on its configuration. When it is set in a Hello packet, the router will send and receive Type-7 LSAs on that interface, and the E-bit must be clear. Two routers will not form an adjacency unless they agree on the N-bit, so a mismatch makes the Hello packet be dropped.

Type-7 LSAs are identical to Type-5 LSAs except that the LSA header type is 7, they are flooded only within the originating NSSA under the same rules as Type-1 and Type-2 LSAs, and they carry a propagate bit (P). When the P-bit is set, an NSSA border router translates the LSA into a Type-5 LSA, and its forwarding address must then be non-zero. The default for the P-bit is clear. The metrics and path types of Type-5 and Type-7 LSAs are directly comparable.

An NSSA ASBR (an AS boundary router) sets the E-bit in its router-LSA, and NSSA ASBRs may only originate Type-7 LSAs into NSSAs. When two NSSA routers originate functionally equivalent Type-7 LSAs, the least preferred one is flushed: a set P-bit wins, and otherwise the higher router ID wins.
sections.eli5: The N-bit is a badge that says we are an NSSA neighborhood, and neighbors without the same badge will not become friends. The P-bit is a sticker that means please share this road with the whole town.

sections.title: Route Calculation and Summary Routes
sections.content:
Routers calculate AS external routes by examining AS-external-LSAs of either Type-5 or Type-7. The procedure is a modest modification of the OSPF specification's section 16.4. Because a Type-7 LSA only floods within its NSSA, its ASBR must be reachable over that NSSA. When two paths are otherwise equal, a Type-7 LSA with the P-bit set is preferred, then a Type-5 LSA, then the LSA with the higher router ID. An NSSA border router does not install a Type-7 default route whose P-bit is clear.

Importing OSPF summary routes into an NSSA as Type-3 summary-LSAs is optional, controlled by the ImportSummaries parameter, and the default is enabled. When summaries are not imported, the default LSA a border router sends into the NSSA must be a Type-3 summary-LSA. This stops intra-AS traffic from leaving the AS through a Type-7 default route from an NSSA internal router.
sections.eli5: When a router picks the best road, it looks at the usual things first, like how short it is. If two roads tie, special tie-breaker rules decide, like who has the bigger name tag.

sections.title: Translating Type-7 LSAs into Type-5 LSAs
sections.content:
Normally only one NSSA border router needs to translate, because extra translators unnecessarily grow the link state database. The area parameter NSSATranslatorRole is either Always (translate regardless of other routers) or Candidate (take part in an election, which is the default). In the election, a border router stays disabled if another reachable border router has the Nt bit set in its router-LSA or has a higher router ID, and otherwise it is elected. A deposed translator keeps working for TranslatorStabilityInterval, whose default is 40 seconds, to avoid excessive flushing.

A Type-7 LSA is translated only if its P-bit is set, its forwarding address is not 0.0.0.0 and it is not covered by a DoNotAdvertise address range. A translated Type-5 LSA copies the network, mask, path type, metric, forwarding address and route tag of the Type-7 LSA. If a Type-7 address range covers several routes, a single aggregated Type-5 LSA is generated instead, with forwarding address 0.0.0.0. If any covered route has path type 2, the range gets path type 2 with the highest Type-2 cost plus 1. Otherwise it gets path type 1 with the highest cost. For example, Type-7 routes with costs 10 and 11 (type 1) and a type 2 cost of 5 yield a Type-5 LSA of path type 2 and metric 6.
sections.eli5: Only one gatekeeper needs to repaint the roads, so the neighborhood picks one. If the gatekeeper leaves, the next one waits a little before taking over so things stay calm.

sections.title: Security Considerations and the P-bit Paradox
sections.content:
The RFC notes that routing protocols face two kinds of issues: authentication of routing information, and denial of service from repeated or excessive advertisements. Both exist independently of NSSA support. OSPF's own authentication covers the first, with the Cryptographic option being believed secure against passive attacks. OSPF limits repetition by allowing a new LSA instance to be originated once every MinLSInterval (5 seconds) and accepted once every MinLSArrival (1 second). Configuring stub areas and NSSAs can also help routers with limited resources when the link state database grows large.

Appendix E describes the P-bit policy paradox. Non-default Type-7 LSAs with the P-bit clear can be installed on NSSA border routers, yet are not propagated as Type-5 LSAs. Traffic from outside the NSSA that passes through a border router may therefore be diverted into the NSSA, contrary to the path its source expected and to the policy implied by the clear P-bit.
sections.eli5: If one gatekeeper keeps a secret shortcut that the rest of the town does not know about, drivers who pass by might get steered down it by surprise.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 1587
sections.content:
Appendix F lists what changed from RFC 1587. All differences are backward-compatible.

  • Importing summary routes became optional (it was mandatory in RFC 1587).
  • Setting of the forwarding address in Type-7 LSAs was refined.
  • The Type-7 route calculation now includes the path preference of the OSPF specification, and a Type-7 default route with the P-bit clear is not installed on a border router.
  • The translator election was updated to close a bug when the highest-router-ID translator loses connectivity to the transit topology, and the translator can be configured, with more than one allowed.
  • A deposed translator flushes aggregated Type-5 LSAs, and the P-bit default was defined as clear.
sections.eli5: This is the list of fixes and new options compared with the older rule book. Old and new neighborhoods can still be neighbors.

viz.caption: OPTION BITS USED BY NSSAS (RFC 3101, APPENDIX A)

items.label: E-bit
items.desc: Clear in Hello means no Type-5 LSAs are sent or received on the interface (stub area or NSSA).

items.label: N-bit
items.desc: Set in Hello means Type-7 LSAs are sent and received. Neighbors must agree. If set, E must be clear.

items.label: P-bit
items.desc: In the Type-7 LSA header. Flags the border router to translate it into a Type-5 LSA. Default is clear.
